newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada quarterly earnings marred by commodities.
newsitem.headline: Canada quarterly earnings marred by commodities.

text.p: Canada's robust economy will boost corporate profits in the second-quarter earnings season, but limp commodity prices are expected to mar the performance of Canadian resource companies.
Analysts expect double-digit profit growth in most sectors when second-quarter earnings roll out over the next few weeks, but the outlook for resources remains cloudy.

"We're looking for all 300 (Toronto Stock Exchange Composite Index) companies to be up 21 percent (on a year-on-year per share basis)," said Diane Urquhart, head of equity research at ScotiaMcLeod Inc.
She said profits would be dragged down by dismal results in the forestry sector and mixed performances by the gold, metals and oil industry.
"We're expecting most (forestry) companies to report losses and more than 100 percent declines from the prior years," Urquhart said.

The forestry sector, which was hit in 1996 by falling newsprint and pulp prices that never recovered, would end the year lower but improve on a quarter-over-quarter basis and see a "major rebound" in 1998, she predicted.
The gold and metals sectors were also expected to post losses. Analysts said the situation would worsen through 1997 if gold prices extended their current slide.

"Precious metals will look bad. With the weakness in the gold market we're not going to see anything dramatic in that area. And the metals are still sluggish," said Peter Chandler, senior vice-president of C.M. Oliver & Co. Ltd.
Chandler and Urquhart agreed that one bright spot would be the steel industry, which could see profit growth of up to 35 percent in the quarter.

The commodity downswing has spilled over into the energy sector, with crude oil and natural gas prices dipping 20 to 26 percent since the start of the year. But analysts said the sector, which had resisted the resource malaise in previous quarters, did better than its natural resource rivals.

"I'd look for the growth in their profits to soften a bit in the second quarter. But overall that sector is still quite a bit more healthy than other resource producers, and I don't expect that to change in the second half of the year," said Doug Porter, an economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns.
Analysts said soft earnings by export-oriented companies should be outweighed by strong domestic growth.
Urquhart reckoned the communications sector should see profit growth of about 25 percent in the quarter, while banks and merchandising could both be up by about 18 percent.
Porter said the current climate of low inflation, low interest rates and improving growth boded well for Canada's banks, which have enjoyed three years of record earnings.
"They are also being helped by the ongoing tremendous interest in the equity market that helps their investment banking arms and the sale of mutal funds as well," he said.
Domestic growth was also expected to boost profits among some industrials and consumer products producers.

"Consumer spending has really picked up the pace in the last three months. That's evident whether you look at home sales or department store sales or auto sales, all of them are posting double-digit growth," said Porter.
Chandler agreed: "Anything involved with the construction industry should be doing reasonably well, so building suppliers, building-related materials, should show reasonably good earnings as well."
